Temporal patterns of charging events for batteries responding to the SCE Large C&I price profile in the 2030 low price forecast scenario. Note that times are shown in standard time, such that a 7am summer charging event would be beginning at 8am local clock time The optimal behavior of the battery is further illustrated in Figure 32, which shows the average daily charging and discharging pattern. For a given tariff design scenario, the differences in battery response are very modest (across utility, customer class, and price forecast scenarios). There is a bit more variation in behavior across tariff designs, but in general the temporal patterns are the same. In all scenarios, the batteries tend to charge from midnight to 4am, discharge from 4am to 7am, then charge again from 7 or 8am to 2pm. They then do an evening discharge from 4pm to 7pm, before sitting idle the rest of the evening. In the Medium and Mild scenario, the morning discharge tends to start a little later, and the evening discharge a little earlier. This is likely due to bias in the days when the batteries do not cycle (as discussed, there are fewer cycles per year under these scenarios) rather than differences in the daily price shape. Figure 32. Average daily charge/discharge profile for battery responding to various price signals (tariff design as panels, utilities and customer class as lines) in the 2030 low price forecast As discussed, the battery dispatch behavior varies somewhat across tariff design scenarios (Full, Medium, Mild), cycling less on the more mild shapes, but does not vary much across other price profile descriptors. However, when looking at the revenues these batteries earn from their cycling, results are extremely sensitive to price scenarios across almost all scenario dimensions. Figure 33 and Table 9 show the revenue per kW of battery that the BESS earns by responding to the dynamic price for the entire year, in nominal 2030 dollars. The highest revenues of $221-269/kW-yr are awarded to batteries responding to a residential tariff, in the 49 high price forecast, with the Full dynamic tariff design. Residential customers pay more for electricity on a per-kWh basis, relative to non-residential customers, and therefore the revenue the BESS earns for discharging at high price times is significantly more than other customer classes. Large C&I customer batteries would earn $136-190/kW-yr in the same price forecast and tariff design scenario. Switching to the low price forecast limits these earnings substantially, except for SDG&E customers whose prices are similar in the two scenarios. In the low price forecast Full tariff scenario, PG&E and SCE residential batteries would earn around $120/kW-yr. Revenue potential is somewhat limited in the Medium tariff design scenario, and is substantially lowered in the Mild tariff scenario; at most, residential and large C&I batteries earn $72 and $53, respectively, per kW-yr, and in the low price forecast case, these earnings can be as small as $15 per year.
